verses.text: In those days Hezekiah was sick and dying. Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, “Yahweh says, ‘Set your house in order; for you will die, and not live.’”
Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed to Yahweh, saying,
“Remember now, Yahweh, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Before Isaiah had gone out into the middle part of the city, Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,

“Turn back, and tell Hezekiah the prince of my people, ‘Yahweh, the God of David your father, says, “I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you. On the third day, you will go up to Yahweh’s house.
I will add to your days fifteen years. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for my own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.”’”
Isaiah said, “Take a cake of figs.” They took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered.
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “What will be the sign that Yahweh will heal me, and that I will go up to Yahweh’s house the third day?”
Isaiah said, “This will be the sign to you from Yahweh, that Yahweh will do the thing that he has spoken: should the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah answered, “It is a light thing for the shadow to go forward ten steps. No, but let the shadow return backward ten steps.”
Isaiah the prophet cried to Yahweh; and he brought the shadow ten steps backward, by which it had gone down on the sundial of Ahaz.
At that time Berodach Baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah; for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.

Hezekiah listened to them, and showed them all the storehouse of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, and the house of his armor, and all that was found in his treasures. There was nothing in his house, or in all his dominion, that Hezekiah didn’t show them.
Then Isaiah the prophet came to king Hezekiah, and said to him, “What did these men say? From where did they come to you?” Hezekiah said, “They have come from a far country, even from Babylon.”
He said, “What have they seen in your house?” Hezekiah answered, “They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing among my treasures that I have not shown them.”
Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear Yahweh’s word.
‘Behold, the days come that all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have laid up in store to this day, will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left,’ says Yahweh.
‘They will take away some of your sons who will issue from you, whom you will father; and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.’”
Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “Yahweh’s word which you have spoken is good.” He said moreover, “Isn’t it so, if peace and truth will be in my days?”

Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Hezekiah lies dying, and the Lord sends Isaiah not with comfort but with stark truth: "Set your house in order." The honesty of it strikes me—God doesn't hide hard things from His people. Yet in that very directness, there's mercy, for it turns Hezekiah's face back to the One who made him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dark of his sickroom, Hezekiah turns to face the wall—turning away from the world's noise to pray. Sometimes our turning away from all else is what opens us to hear the Lord most clearly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart." Hezekiah's prayer isn't boastful—it's the honest assessment of one who has tried to walk faithfully. And his tears flow freely; he weeps not from doubt but from a heart that loves the God he's served.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah hasn't even left the city when the Lord speaks. No delay, no waiting—the prayer of a faithful heart rises and the answer comes before the prophet even reaches the streets. That's how eager our Father is to hear His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears." Those two simple phrases—the Lord has *heard* and *seen*—carry all the tenderness of a Father bending down to His child. Hezekiah will live, will worship in the temple on the third day, and the Lord's compassion is as real as the healing itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifteen more years added to Hezekiah's life, and the promise to protect Jerusalem—not because Hezekiah deserves it, but for David's sake and the Lord's own name's sake. Grace always points beyond us, to the One who gives it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A cake of figs laid on the boil—such a simple remedy, such an ordinary thing. Yet it works, and healing comes through the means the Lord provides. The Lord meets us both in the miraculous and in the everyday kindness of a poultice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah asks for a sign. It's not doubt—it's the request of one who wants to know that the promise is real and sealed. We all long for that kind of certainty sometimes; the Lord is patient with our needing to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah offers a choice: shall the shadow move forward or back? A test of faith—which would be harder to believe? Either way, the sign is the Lord's to give, not the shadow's to choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah chooses the harder sign—the shadow going backward, against nature. He's saying, "If You're going to show me, show me something that only You can do." That's the language of someone learning to ask for the kind of work only God can accomplish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shadow on Ahaz's sundial moves backward—time itself obeys the Lord's word. Isaiah cries out, and the impossible happens. I've always loved that the Lord doesn't just promise healing; He gives a sign written in light and shadow, something Hezekiah can see with his own eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Berodach Baladan sends letters and gifts—he's heard that the great king of Judah lay sick but recovered. The news travels, and even distant kingdoms notice when the Lord works. Yet this messenger will become a test of Hezekiah's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah listens to the Babylonian visitors and shows them *everything*—his silver, gold, spices, armor, treasures. He holds nothing back. Pride can creep in even after healing; he wants the world to see how blessed and powerful he is, and he forgets whom those blessings came from.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah asks the hard question: "What did these men say? Where did they come from?" His tone is gentle but direct—he's drawing Hezekiah to see what his own heart has done. A true prophet doesn't flatter; he loves enough to ask the questions that lead to repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing among my treasures that I have not shown them." Hezekiah's admission is matter-of-fact, almost proud still—he hasn't yet grasped what his openness has invited into Jerusalem.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Hear Yahweh's word." Isaiah speaks as he always has, with no anger but with the gravity of one who carries the Lord's message. What comes next will be hard, but it comes from love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All that Hezekiah has shown will one day be carried away to Babylon. Not lost, but taken—the very treasures he displayed with pride will become spoil. It's a hard mercy: the Lord shows him now what will come, that he might repent and take it to heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His own sons will be taken to serve in Babylon's palace. The wound cuts deep—not just loss of treasure, but of his own lineage. Yet even this word is meant as correction, a call to return his heart to the God who alone is worthy of allegiance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah's response is humble and strange: "Yahweh's word which you have spoken is good." He accepts the hard word, then adds, "Isn't it so, if peace and truth will be in my days?" He's repented and found grace—the judgment will come, but not in his lifetime. That's mercy too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pool and conduit Hezekiah made still stand—engineering and foresight that served his people well. The chronicler preserves it not as a boast but as part of a king's legacy. Wisdom and provision, even when pride has been corrected, remain good works.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah sleeps with his fathers, and Manasseh reigns in his place. Readers today hear an echo in this: the faithful king goes to his rest, and the kingdom passes on. Yet we know—looking back—that the warnings Hezekiah heard would shape all that followed. Our choices ripple forward into generations we'll never see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
